cases.abstract: Conformal prediction addresses whether a set contains the target, whereas segmentation and other tasks also require control of graded errors. Conformal risk control extends calibration to expected loss by reserving a worst-case contribution for the unseen observation before choosing among nested prediction sets. For n calibration observations, the rule bounds expected test loss by alpha when the losses are exchangeable, non-increasing, right-continuous, bounded above by B, and admit a safe maximal parameter. This guarantee averages over calibration and test data rather than applying to each realized split. If the losses are also independent, identically distributed, and nonnegative, with no discontinuity at any fixed parameter value almost surely, expected loss is at least alpha - 2B/(n+1); the gap is sharp for general monotone losses. Monotonicity is consequential: bounded non-monotone losses can make the same rule incur expected loss arbitrarily close to B. Applications to segmentation, multilabel classification, hierarchical classification, and question answering produce average risks near their targets over 1,000 random splits. Together, the bounds and examples establish calibration beyond binary coverage while showing why boundedness alone cannot ensure risk control.
cases.methods: For n calibration observations, write R_n(lambda) for the mean loss and let B bound each loss from above. The rule takes the infimum of parameters satisfying [n R_n(lambda) + B]/(n+1) <= alpha, using the safe maximal parameter if none qualifies. Reserving B for the unseen case makes the corrected calibration average dominate the average that would include its actual loss. The proof compares this implementable choice with an infeasible threshold computed symmetrically from all n+1 loss functions. The corrected choice is at least as large, so non-increasing losses give it no greater test loss. Conditional on the unordered collection, exchangeability makes the expected held-out loss equal the full-sample average at the symmetric threshold; right-continuity ensures that threshold achieves the target. Thus the correction controls expected loss over calibration and test randomness without requiring the test outcome during calibration.
cases.results: On polyp segmentation and MS COCO, mean false-negative risks are 0.0987 and 0.0996 against a target of 0.1, with standard deviations across 1,000 random splits of 0.0114 and 0.0052. These averages support near-target calibration, although individual splits can exceed the target. Calibration sizes differ, at 1,000 and 4,000 observations, so the narrower COCO distribution cannot be attributed solely to the application. Hierarchical ImageNet yields a mean normalized distance loss of 0.0499, with a between-split standard deviation of 0.0011, at a target of 0.05; predictions are almost always at leaf resolution. This example shows that controlling a graded error need not uniformly replace specific predictions with coarse ones. The counterexample marks the structural boundary: without monotonicity, the same rule can yield expected loss arbitrarily close to its upper bound B. Under the other required conditions, taking each loss's supremum over larger parameter values restores control, but substantial non-monotonicity can make that repair conservative.
cases.notes: Theorems 1-2 and Proposition 2 support the risk guarantee, sharp gap, and monotonicity boundary; Figures 1-3 support the selected application findings. The numerical uncertainties are standard deviations across random splits, not confidence intervals. Expected risk averages calibration and test randomness. The question-answering threshold runs opposite to the theorem's parameter direction, so its formula is omitted rather than reproduced without reparameterization. Distribution-shift extensions require specified information about the shift; no validity under an unknown shift is claimed.

cases.abstract: Refitting a prediction model and its calibration scores does not necessarily preserve coverage under distribution shift. Adaptive conformal inference adjusts the nominal miscoverage parameter after each revealed outcome: a miss lowers it to favor larger subsequent sets, while coverage raises it. Calibrating the quantile argument in this way avoids specifying a model of the shift. With a positive fixed step size and quantile conventions allowing whole-space or empty sets, long-run miscoverage frequency converges to the target for any data sequence. This guarantee does not establish coverage at each time. A hidden Markov analysis, with joint stationarity of the environment and adaptive parameter, fixed score and quantile functions, and additional regularity assumptions, provides concentration and mean squared marginal miscoverage bounds that depend on environmental persistence and shifts in the optimal calibration parameter. Volatility forecasting and county-level election prediction show improved local coverage relative to fixed nominal calibration. However, using unnormalized volatility residuals produces much wider coverage swings despite adaptation. The experiments therefore qualify the reach of feedback: local performance depends on score design, while the step size trades responsiveness against stability. The method requires an outcome at every step.
cases.methods: At time t, form the prediction set from responses whose current score is at most Q_t(1-alpha_t). After observing Y_t, encode a miss as err_t = 1 and coverage as err_t = 0, then update alpha_{t+1} = alpha_t + gamma(alpha-err_t). A miss lowers the parameter to favor larger sets; coverage raises it. This operation calibrates the quantile argument and can accompany updates to the score and quantile functions themselves. With gamma > 0, alpha_1 in [0,1], and out-of-range quantile conventions producing whole-space or empty sets, alpha_t remains in [-gamma,1+gamma] without clipping. Summing the recursion expresses cumulative excess miscoverage as (alpha_1-alpha_{T+1})/gamma. Boundedness therefore limits absolute frequency deviation to (max{alpha_1,1-alpha_1}+gamma)/(gamma T), regardless of the data-generating process. This explains the long-run guarantee, but not accurate coverage within every short window.
cases.results: In volatility forecasting, feedback improves local coverage beyond the rolling refitting used by both methods. Both use GARCH forecasts and score calibration based on 1,250 trading days; at gamma = 0.005, adaptation keeps 500-day local coverage near 90%, while fixed nominal calibration has large excursions, including undercoverage for Fannie Mae during the 2008 crisis. The four displayed stocks were selected for clear fixed-calibration failures among twelve examined; favorable adaptive coverage was reported for all twelve. The score comparison qualifies this finding: removing normalization by predicted volatility leads to much wider coverage swings even with feedback, so adaptation does not preserve comparable local coverage across these score choices. In the election study, adaptive calibration keeps 300-county local coverage approximately at 90%, whereas fixed calibration develops troughs around time-zone transitions. Counties were ordered by time zone and randomized within zones, not replayed in actual reporting order. These local improvements are empirical findings in the tested sequences, not consequences of the unrestricted long-run frequency guarantee.
cases.notes: Proposition 4.1 supports accumulated frequency control, not timewise coverage or interval efficiency. The stronger hidden Markov results require stationarity of the joint environment-parameter process and fixed score and quantile functions; concentration additionally uses a positive spectral gap, and the marginal error bound assumes Lipschitz miscoverage and attainable interior targets. These results do not automatically cover the rolling refits. Figures 1-2 supply the matched calibration and score contrasts; the displayed stocks are selected failure cases. Figure 3 uses geographic ordering rather than an election-night replay. No interval-width gain is asserted.
